Quiz – well, box, caisson
What takes the shell of a well or box foundation down into the depth?
Its own weight, while the soil is removed from inside
Hydraulic jacks pressing it down
Vibration, as with sheet piles
The buoyancy of the groundwater
The reinforced concrete shell sinks under its own weight, while the “clamshell” grab removes the soil from inside – and from under the cutting edge. Buoyancy works against it.
What is the typical size of well foundations?
Diameter 0.8–3.0 m, length 4–8 m
Diameter 10–30 cm, length 20–30 m
Diameter 20–60 m, length 40–50 m
Diameter 5–6 m, length 1–2 m
The well foundation supports columns and walls at discrete points: Ø 0.8–3.0 m, 4–8 m long; at the top they are tied together by a reinforced concrete grillage or slab.
How can the shell friction of a well be reduced?
With bentonite slurry or single-sized rounded gravel, or with a shoulder offset
With denser reinforcement
By omitting the cutting edge
By raising the groundwater table
Because of the shoulder offset and the tapered shape, the cutting edge cuts a larger hole than the shell; thixotropic slurry or rolling gravel can be placed in the gap.
What was the highest excess pressure used in caissons?
Approx. 10 m of water column = 1 bar, so 3.2–3.5 bar corresponds roughly to 32–35 m of water depth – people cannot work at higher pressure.
Why did the caisson have two airlocks?
One for people (slow pressure change), one for materials and the excavated soil
One for the entrance, one for the emergency exit
One for compressed air, one for water
Because it had two working chambers
In the personnel airlock the pressure was changed slowly, over hours (caisson disease!); the soil and materials were moved through a separate airlock.
What is the plan of a box foundation?
The same as the plan of the structure (e.g. bridge pier, building)
Point-like, under the columns
Always circular
The same as the plan of the pile grillage
The wells support at discrete points, the box goes under the whole structure – which is why it is much larger.
How is the sinking of an open box organised?
In stages: it is built and sunk in stages of 6–8 m, with cross walls inside
It is built to its full height in one piece, then sunk in a single step
The pit is excavated first and the box lifted into it
By floating, on the water
One stage is 6–8 m; a larger cutting edge all round at the bottom, stiffening cross walls inside. In easily dredged soil it gets down as far as 40–50 m.
What is the greatest danger when sinking a box?
Tilting, which can cause irreparable jamming
The concrete setting too fast
The box floating up
Even sinking is very difficult; continuous monitoring is needed. If the soil loosens, a subsidence crater may also form in the surroundings.
What do we mean by “well foundation” today?
An excavated foundation with a recoverable steel casing
A masonry well built of well rings
A dug well for drinking water
A diaphragm wall box
A steel casing is vibrated down while the soil is continuously removed, then the well is concreted through a tremie pipe while the casing is withdrawn.
